turns.prompt_text: This pot is $5, and appears to be iron Attached 1 file. - ba982a31-aae4-4f84-a8e3-a835493c9efc
turns.response_html:
That pot is actually cast aluminum, not iron.

While the weight and thickness can mimic cast iron, that distinctive chalky, matte-grey finish is a telltale sign of heavy aluminum oxidation.

What Happened to It?

The pot most likely went through a dishwasher. Standard dishwasher detergents are highly alkaline and react with raw or anodized aluminum, causing it to "bloom" with that grey, powdery residue. This oxidation is safe but can rub off onto your hands or food, giving it a metallic taste.

Is It Worth the $5?

It’s a solid deal if you don’t mind a little elbow grease. Aluminum is an excellent heat conductor (much faster than iron), and these older "hand-poured" or cast aluminum pots are durable workhorses.

How to restore it:

  • The Acid Bath: Fill the pot with water and add 2 tablespoons of cream of tartar or white vinegar per quart of water. Bring it to a boil for 10–15 minutes. The acid will "eat" the oxidation and brighten the metal.
  • Abrasives: For the outside, you can use a fine steel wool pad (like Brillo or S.O.S.) with some soapy water. It will bring back the silver luster fairly quickly.
  • Maintenance: Never put it in the dishwasher again—hand wash only!

The Quick "Thrift Store" Test

If you want to be 100% sure before you buy:

  1. The Magnet Test: A magnet will snap onto cast iron but will completely ignore aluminum.
  2. The Handle: Notice the rivets holding the handle on. Cast iron is almost always cast as a single solid piece (including the handle), whereas aluminum often uses steel rivets to attach a separate handle.

Since it’s in Ames, if you’re looking for something that holds heat better for a long braise, keep hunting for a heavy Lodge; but if you want a lightweight, fast-heating pot for sauces or grains, this one will clean up nicely.

What are you planning to cook in it?

turns.prompt_text: Would it make a good cauldron? for glass or other clay/ceramics?
turns.response_html:
For glass or ceramics? Definitely not.

While it looks rugged, using this as a crucible for melting glass or firing clay would likely end in a molten mess on your floor. Here is the technical breakdown of why this pot won't survive those temperatures:

The Thermal Limits

Aluminum has a relatively low melting point compared to the materials you're interested in:

  • Aluminum melting point: ~$1,221^{\circ}F$ ($660^{\circ}C$)
  • Glass melting point: ~$2,400^{\circ}F$ ($1,300^{\circ}C$+)
  • Ceramic firing (Cone 06-10): $1,800^{\circ}F$ to $2,350^{\circ}F$ ($1,000^{\circ}C$ to $1,300^{\circ}C$)

The Verdict: If you tried to melt glass in this, the pot would liquefy and collapse long before the glass even began to soften.

What it can handle

If you want to use it for "cauldron-adjacent" maker projects, it’s great for low-temp materials:

  • Wax (Candle making): Perfect. Aluminum distributes heat evenly, preventing "hot spots" that flash-ignite wax.
  • Soap Making: Excellent for lye solutions (though the aluminum will react and darken further, it's a common "sacrificial" vessel).
  • Pewter or Lead: Aluminum can technically hold molten lead or pewter (which melt around $621^{\circ}F$), but it's risky because you are getting close to the point where the aluminum loses its structural integrity.

Better Alternatives

If you are looking to get into DIY glass or ceramic work:

  1. For Glass: You need a refractory kiln and graphite or stainless steel molds/crucibles specifically rated for high heat.
  2. For Clay: You can do "pit firing" in your backyard using nothing but a hole in the ground and sawdust, but a metal pot isn't used because the metal would scale, flake, and melt in the embers.
  3. For Metal Casting: If you want a "cauldron" for melting stuff, look for a graphite-clay crucible. They are inexpensive and designed to handle $3,000^{\circ}F$ safely.
